$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "ea1605db-abbe-5c50-acc7-74e45ebbde3f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1876 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186074957 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we'll consider real-life situations where we have to multiply fractions by whole numbers.

Suppose that Justin, a chef, has $8$ large tins of tomatoes. If each tin of tomatoes weighs $\dfrac{5}{4}\,\textrm{lb},$ how many pounds of tomatoes does Justin have in total?

To find out the total weight of tomatoes, we need to multiply $\dfrac{5}{4}\,\textrm{lb}$ by $8.$  

To multiply a fraction by a whole number, we multiply the fraction's numerator by the whole number and keep the denominator the same:

$$
8 \times \dfrac54= \dfrac{8\times 5}{4} = \dfrac{40}4
$$

We can simplify this fraction by interpreting the fraction as a division:

$$
\dfrac{40}{4} =  40 \operatorname{div}  4 = 10
$$

So, in total, Justin has $10\,\textrm{lb}$ of tomatoes." :tutorial/id #uuid "298ab81d-8afe-5255-bdcd-354d669f8700" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1886 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186074962 :tutorial/content "There are many ways to divide decimals. One such way is to write the division as a fraction and then multiply the numerator and denominator by a power of $10$ so that both become whole numbers. Then, we carry out the division as usual.

To illustrate, let's use this method to find the value of $4.5\operatorname{div}  0.5$.

**Step 1.** First, we write the division problem as a fraction:

$$
\dfrac{4.5}{0.5}
$$

**Step 2.** Then, we multiply the numerator and denominator by $10$:

$$
\dfrac{4.5\times 10}{0.5\times 10} = \dfrac{45}{5}
$$

**Step 3.** Finally, we solve the resulting division problem. In this case, we have

$$
45 \operatorname{div}  5 = 9
$$

Therefore,

$$
4.5 \operatorname{div}  0.5 = 9 \,
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "a797dd04-1427-5605-9e35-c8a266fa5173" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1960 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186074963 :tutorial/content "When using long division to divide whole numbers, it's often appropriate to round the final answer.

For instance, let's find the value of $58 \operatorname{div}  7$, rounded to the nearest tenth. We start by going through the long division procedure as usual:

| $\,\, \phantom{0} {\:\phantom{\mid}} 8 {\,. \,} 2 {\:\phantom{\mid}} {\color{black}8} \: \ldots$$7$$\phantom{\mid}\!\!\!\enclose{longdiv}{5 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 8 {\,. \,} 0 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 0}$$-\!\!\!$$5$$6$$2$$0$$-\!\!\!$$1$$4$$6$$0$$-\!\!\!$$5$$6$$4$$\vdots$ |
| --- |

We could divide further, but since we want to round to $1$ decimal place (the nearest tenth), we stop after finding the quotient to $2$ decimal places:

$$
58 \operatorname{div}  7 = 8.28 \ldots
$$

Finally, we round the quotient to the nearest tenth. The hundredths place is $8$, which is greater than $5$, so we round up:
$8.28 \ldots \rightarrow 8.3$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5f74891d-a04f-506e-a1d4-72f98dfc5324" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1962 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186074964 :tutorial/content "We can use the standard algorithm to divide decimals by whole numbers.

To illustrate, let's compute $7.2 \operatorname{div}  3$.

First, we write down the problem using long division notation, keeping the decimal point in the dividend:

| $3$$\!\enclose{longdiv}{7 {\,\bbox[2px, lightgray]{\color{blue}.}\,} 2}{\:\phantom{\mid}}$ |
| --- |

We also bring the decimal point up into the quotient, placing it directly above the decimal point in the dividend:

| $\,\phantom{0} \bbox[2px, lightgray]{\color{blue}.}$$3$$\!\enclose{longdiv}{7 {\bbox[2px, lightgray]{\color{blue}.} 2{\:\phantom{\mid}}}}$ |
| --- |

Now, we carry out the long division process as usual:

| $\,2 {\,\,. \,} 4$$3$$\!\enclose{longdiv}{7 {\,\,. \,} 2}$$-\!\!\!\!\!$$6$$1$$2$$-\!\!\!\!\!$$1$$2$$0$ |
| --- |

Therefore,

$$
7.2 \operatorname{div}  3 = 2.4 \,
$$

**Note:** The "standard algorithm" is the same as "long division." The two phrases can be used interchangeably." :tutorial/id #uuid "2d1369fc-bc3a-5c6e-b61f-4eca77f96da0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1963 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186074965 :tutorial/content "We can also use the standard algorithm to divide decimals by other decimals. The only difference is that we first need to find an equivalent division problem where the divisor is a whole number.

To illustrate, let's compute $1.11\operatorname{div}  0.3 \,$. First, we write this division problem as a fraction:

$$
\dfrac{1.11}{0.3}
$$

Then, we multiply the numerator and denominator by $10$ so that we get a whole number in the denominator:

$$
\dfrac{1.11 \times 10}{0.3\times 10} = \dfrac{11.1}{3}
$$

Now we see that the division problem is equivalent to $11.1 \operatorname{div}  3$. We can compute this using long division as usual:

| $\,\, 0 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 3 {\,\,. \,} 7$$3$$\!\enclose{longdiv}{1 {\:\phantom{\mid}} 1 {\,\,. \,} 1}$$-\!\!\!\!\!$$9$$2$$1$$-\!\!\!\!\!$$2$$1$$0$ |
| --- |

From the long division, we find that

$$
11.1 \operatorname{div}  3 = 3.7
$$

so we conclude that

$$
1.11 \operatorname{div}  0.3 = 3.7 \,
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "53648922-c8dc-502d-af90-e2fcd1b0808f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1964 :tutorial/title "Dividing Decimals Using the Standard Algorithm"} {:db/id 17592186074970 :tutorial/content "A **unit rate** is a comparison of two quantities where one of the terms has a quantity of $1.$ This means the ratio, in fraction form, has a denominator of $1.$

For instance, suppose Michael earned $\$ 200$ by selling $4$ identical tires.

The ratio of dollars to tires is ${\color{blue}200}:{\color{red}4}.$ Writing the ratio as a fraction, we have

$$
\dfrac{{\color{blue}200}}{{\color{red}4}} \, .
$$

The unit rate is how many dollars Michael got for $1$ tire.

We can make a denominator of $1$ by dividing the numerator and denominator by $4\mathbin{:}$

$$
\dfrac{{\color{blue}200} \operatorname{div}  4}{{\color{red}4} \operatorname{div}  4} = \dfrac{{\color{blue}50}}{{\color{red}1}}
$$

This is the unit rate. In this case, we say that Michael got $\color{blue}50$ dollars *per* tire." :tutorial/id #uuid "0bf127db-09c1-53b5-b2fa-6f6520b032f8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2055 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186074971 :tutorial/content "In some tape diagrams, each box can represent more than one unit.

For instance, the ratio of pins to paper clips in a case is given by the tape diagram below. If there are $15$ pins in the case, how many paper clips are there in total?

![](images/82/82f94d7377ea3923ffdd825de324b128cd8b4f102070bf6890dee2cbc619657e.png)

We are told that there are $15$ pins in the case, but the tape diagram for pins shows $3$ boxes. Therefore, each box in the diagram above represents $15 \operatorname{div}  3 = 5$ units. 

Now, we fill the number $5$ in each box of both tapes:

![](images/7d/7d8d1e22ee067588593b7b08442dd2a44142f9f684d84809056ee0ffb4b2dfc0.png)

Since there are $4$ boxes corresponding to paper clips, and each box represents $5$ units, the total number of paper clips is

$$
4 \times 5 = 20 \, .
$$

So, there are $20$ paper clips in Mrs. Robinson's case." :tutorial/id #uuid "6a5fc255-be3d-58ad-b9c5-c1bbed5b72ad" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2056 :tutorial/title "Computing Ratios Using Tape Diagrams With Multiple Units"} {:db/id 17592186075004 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we will learn how to divide larger numbers by two-digit numbers *with remainders* using the relationship between multiplication and division.

To begin with, let's figure out how to compute $47\operatorname{div}  13$.

We will start by computing products of $13$ and other whole numbers, starting from $1$, until we get to a number that is greater than $47$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
13 \cdot 1 &= 13 \\
13 \cdot 2 &= 13 + 13 = 26 \\
13 \cdot 3 &= 26 + 13 = 39✓ \\
13 \cdot 4 &= 39 + 13 = 52\cdot(> {47}, so too big)
\end{aligned}
$$

So, $13 \times {\color{blue}3}$ is *smaller than* $47$, but $13 \times 4$ is *greater than* $47$. This means that ${47}\operatorname{div}  {13}$ has a whole number part (or quotient) of ${\color{blue}3}$.

To find the remainder, we subtract the product from the dividend:

$$
{47} - {39} = {\color{red}8}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{47}\operatorname{div}  {13} = {\color{blue}3}\,\textrm{R}\,{\color{red}8}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "76b99e7b-d478-5c78-8d1f-0df23c51d018" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3311 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186075018 :tutorial/content "We can use area models to understand what it means to divide a fraction by a whole number.

For example, let's consider the area model below:

![](images/66/664911a4bae7edacdf2b68f8fddb7dd54af3da02ab995c003e9001cd8b27aaff.png)

The area of a rectangle equals its length multiplied by its width.

For the given rectangle:

- its length is $3$
- its width is $\dfrac{1}{12}$
- its area is $\dfrac{1}{4}$

Therefore, this area model shows the following multiplication problem:

$$
3\times \dfrac{1}{12} = \dfrac{1}{4}
$$

Using the relationship between multiplication and division, we can turn this multiplication problem into the following division problem:

$$
\dfrac{1}{12} = \dfrac14\operatorname{div}  3
$$

We can also use area models to interpret the division of a whole number by a fraction. Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "fb50d818-df78-5078-b660-6f8c07ef11c9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6687 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186075044 :tutorial/content "The model below represents $2$ wholes. Let's use it to calculate the value of $2 \operatorname{div}  \dfrac{1}{5}.$

![](images/bc/bceafee7d9ca5e92e69b5d33d9504f4290526b80059ad62ed26229d02712a278.png)

 

To calculate ${\color{red}2} \operatorname{div}  \dfrac{1}{\color{blue}5}$, we need to divide each of $\color{red}2$ wholes into $\color{blue}5$ equal parts, as shown below.

![](images/cf/cf608ce8f5d8e2a47a4bebe21f198d193b10dd8f6e95436986bc954c89c60d19.png)

 

We get ${\color{red}2} \times {\color{blue}5} = 10$ pieces in total. 

Therefore,

$$
2 \operatorname{div}  \dfrac{1}{5} = 10\,.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "2de869cb-775d-5db4-b90d-7df0de218fc0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8561 :tutorial/title "Dividing Whole Numbers by Unit Fractions"} {:db/id 17592186075045 :tutorial/content "To divide a unit fraction by a whole number, we multiply the fraction's denominator by the whole number.

For example, to calculate $\dfrac{1}{5} \operatorname{div}  {\color{blue}2},$ we multiply the fraction's denominator by ${\color{blue}2}\!:$

$$
\dfrac{1}{5} \operatorname{div}  {\color{blue}2}  = \dfrac{1}{5 \times {\color{blue}2}} = \dfrac{1}{10}
$$

Notice that we get the same answer using a fraction model, and the process is similar.

![](images/3f/3f1f0dddd115c0d820de4d79624bd87492e215a6c2de43071fda73a4a0684d77.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "fcf4ea8b-7765-55e8-b5c1-a10899bee9f6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8562 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186075046 :tutorial/content "To divide a whole number by a unit fraction, we can multiply the whole number by the fraction's denominator.

So, to divide $2 \operatorname{div}  \dfrac{1}{\color{blue}5},$ we multiply the $2$ by ${\color{blue}5}\!:$

$$
2 \operatorname{div}  \dfrac{1}{\color{blue}5} = 2 \times {\color{blue}5} = 10
$$

And that's the answer! Notice that this method does the same job as the fraction model method we used before:

![](images/5f/5f2eb6ab39ea67466d7a42a8809b8a039a84f9a20a13cca3659d81f669a772a5.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "058743c7-e03e-521c-92ce-c1a5fd00663f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8572 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186075048 :tutorial/content "We can estimate decimal division by rounding each decimal to the nearest whole number and dividing the resulting numbers.

For example, suppose we wish to estimate the quotient of the following division problem.
$19.7 \operatorname{div}  5.3$

One way to proceed is first to round both quantities to the nearest whole number:

$$
\begin{array}{ccc}19.7 & ÷ & 5.3 \\ ↓ &  & ↓ \\ {\color{blue}{20}} & ÷ & {\color{blue}{5}}\end{array}
$$

So, we can form an estimate of $19.7 \operatorname{div}  5.3$ by evaluating $20 \operatorname{div}  5$.

Computing the quotient of this simplified problem gives

$$
20 \operatorname{div}  5 = 4
$$

Therefore, $19.7 \operatorname{div}  5.3$ is approximately equal to $4$. We can write this symbolically as follows:

$$
19.7 \operatorname{div}  5.3 \approx 4
$$

The symbol

$$
\approx
$$

means "is approximately equal to."" :tutorial/id #uuid "5c7a997b-e3c3-5ff6-a0dc-63838fdbab45" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8661 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186075052 :tutorial/content "Remember that a *unit* fraction is a fraction containing $\color{blue}1$ in the numerator. So, for example, the fractions 

$$
\dfrac{\color{blue}{1}}2, \qquad\dfrac{\color{blue}{1}}{12}
$$
are both unit fractions, whereas 

$$
\dfrac{\color{red}{2}}9, \qquad \dfrac{\color{red}{3}}{5}
$$
are *not* unit fractions.

In this lesson, we will use models to divide unit fractions by whole numbers. 

Let's use a fraction model to find the value of 

$$
\dfrac{1}{2} \operatorname{div}  2.
$$
We start with a square model of $\dfrac12,$ split *vertically*.

![](images/cc/ccfe0f457342c456200c98cfc46e63bdc1153698282085164eeafae5c2092c45.png)

To divide $\dfrac12$ by ${\color{blue}2},$ we split the above whole into $\color{blue}2$ equal parts *horizontally*. Then, we remove any shaded parts that are not in the bottom row.

![](images/79/7940073ba05d3136ee1d465530a60bc3624b7aa06fd7484d30797758a28976d7.png)

From the picture on the right, we obtain that the shaded part represents $\dfrac14$ of the whole.

Therefore,
$$
\dfrac{1}{2} \operatorname{div}  2 = \dfrac{1}{4}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5efb47fa-47c0-50c8-9c53-0a64bfc732ea" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8924 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186075058 :tutorial/content "How do we write

$$
\dfrac{7}{\color{blue}4} + 5
$$

as a mixed number?

Notice that we cannot write

$$
5\,\dfrac 7 4
$$

because

$$
\dfrac 7 4
$$

is an improper fraction. Instead, let's find this sum using the same method as before.

First, we write $5$ as an improper fraction:

$$
\dfrac{5}{1}
$$

Then, we put this fraction over a denominator of $\color{blue}4$ by multiplying the numerator and denominator by ${\color{blue}{4}}$:

$$
\dfrac{5 \times {\color{blue}{4}}}{1 \times{\color{blue}{4}}} = \dfrac{20}{4}
$$

So now, we have to find the following sum:

$$
\dfrac{7}{4} + \dfrac{20}{4}
$$

To add two fractions with like denominators, we add the numerators and keep the denominators the same:

$$
\frac{7}{4} + \frac{20}{4} = \frac{7 + 20}{4} = \frac{27}{4}
$$

Finally, we convert this to a mixed number:

$$
27 \operatorname{div}  4 = 6 \, \textrm{R} \, 3 = 6 \, \dfrac{3}{4}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c2a88636-00da-54bc-b8d0-f5c0289bf1ef" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8976 :tutorial/title "Adding Improper Fractions and Whole Numbers"} {:db/id 17592186078288 :question/id #uuid "b9891d5c-d928-589e-a461-3f0b39fb1b66" :question/math-academy-id "e-4168" :question/problem "Express $S=4+8+12+\cdots+56+60$ in sigma notation." :question/worked-solution "Notice that the terms of the corresponding sequence

$$
4, \quad 8, \quad 12, \quad , \ldots, \quad 56, \quad 60.
$$

 are multiples of $4,$ and since $60\operatorname{div}  4 = 15,$ there are $15$ terms in total. 

Therefore, the $n$th term of the sequence has the form

$$
a_n =4n,
$$

where $n$ ranges from $n=1$ to $n=15\mathbin{.}$ Indeed:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & =4(1)=4 \\ {a}_{2} & =4(2)=8 \\ {a}_{3} & =4(3)=12 \\  & \,\,⋮ \\ {a}_{14} & =4(14)=56 \\ {a}_{15} & =4(15)=60\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
S=4+8+12+\cdots+56+60=\sum_{n=1}^{15} 4n.
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186078318 :question/id #uuid "0c8d49e2-ad48-506c-9db7-76fd755fcc57" :question/math-academy-id "e-4887" :question/problem "Find the value of the expression $\sqrt{ (3^4+7^2-2) \operatorname{div}  2}.$" :question/worked-solution "To evaluate the given expression, we use PEMDAS. In terms of the order of operations: 

- expressions underneath radicals are treated the same as parentheses

- radicals themselves are treated as exponents

Therefore, following the order of operations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{({3}^{4}+{7}^{2}-2)÷2} &= \sqrt{(81+49-2)÷2} \\ &= \sqrt{(130-2)÷2} \\ &= \sqrt{128÷2} \\ &= \sqrt{64} \\ &= \sqrt{8\cdot 8} \\ &= \sqrt{{8}^{2}} \\ &= 8.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186078319 :question/id #uuid "09a1af5e-aa76-5d08-a0f2-bbb3d534250b" :question/math-academy-id "e-4895" :question/problem "Simplify the expression $\sqrt{((5^2-4) \operatorname{div}  3)-2}.$" :question/worked-solution "To simplify the given expression, we use PEMDAS. In terms of the order of operations,

- expressions underneath radicals are treated the same as parentheses, and

- radicals themselves are treated as exponents.

Therefore, following the order of operations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{(({5}^{2}-4)÷3)-2} &= \sqrt{((25-4)÷3)-2} \\ &= \sqrt{(21÷3)-2} \\ &= \sqrt{7-2} \\ &= \sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186078910 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "91058a51-0523-5e03-bb05-4948d8f59479" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{43}{4}" :db/id 17592186076239} {:answer/id #uuid "bb878f41-a7a3-5d01-a410-267f4eba0d6e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186076240} {:answer/id #uuid "2dc0e83b-f8eb-59c4-ba46-21052b1a466c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4" :db/id 17592186076241} {:answer/id #uuid "5f3e487e-84b9-5344-a367-f9573bb27ce7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186076242} {:answer/id #uuid "5feec12c-b998-5ae1-85a0-363aaf25967e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{29}{4}" :db/id 17592186076243}] :answer-field/id #uuid "0f7f16ae-1cbd-5e46-89aa-1bb598645888" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186076238}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "2e52c627-fb0c-52bc-8264-c98fa175b03c" :question/math-academy-id "q-43667" :question/problem "Find the value of $(\sqrt{81} + 7) \operatorname{div}  (2 - 6)$."} {:db/id 17592186079184 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8e73e610-3db3-532a-85a4-67365caf6e2c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1.899" :db/id 17592186077883} {:answer/id #uuid "94d6848e-7436-5783-b894-91c29417e4f8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-0.145" :db/id 17592186077884} {:answer/id #uuid "ceb35004-71ef-5ad0-9c96-4c95fc927574" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1.901" :db/id 17592186077885} {:answer/id #uuid "ea0c537d-0a2c-5e5f-8631-cd883fe6f763" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186077886} {:answer/id #uuid "06ef917f-ac42-596d-b60c-597b1e23f918" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186077887}] :answer-field/id #uuid "8b343f84-992f-5a68-a3c6-bb81a86ae481" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186077882}] :question/id #uuid "0cc5f4b0-76d8-5d82-a816-40c035daf1e7" :question/math-academy-id "q-69198" :question/problem "What is the value of $\sqrt{(24 \operatorname{div}  2) + 12} - 3$ rounded to $3$ decimal places?

> A scientific calculator is required to answer this question." :question/requires-calculator true} {:db/id 17592186079665 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to simplify the following expression:

$$
-3\sqrt{\left(2^4-1\right) \operatorname{div}  3}\,.
$$

The first thing to realize is that there is an invisible multiplication symbol here. The above expression is short for

$$
-3\,{\color{red}{\times}}\,\sqrt{\left(2^4-1\right) \operatorname{div}  3}\,.
$$

When multiplying a radical by a number, we usually omit the additional multiplication symbol.

Now, to simplify the given expression, we use PEMDAS.  In terms of the order of operations:

- Expressions underneath radicals are treated as if they are contained within parentheses (the **P** in **P**EMDAS), so we always deal with this first.

- Radicals themselves are treated as exponents (the **E** in P**E**MDAS).

Therefore, following PEMDAS, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}-3\sqrt{({2}^{4}-1)÷3} &= -3\sqrt{(16-1)÷3} \\ &= -3\sqrt{15÷3} \\ &= -3\sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

And that's our answer! 

To get a numerical approximation, we need to use a calculator. In this case, we get

$$
-3 \sqrt{5} = -3\times \sqrt{5} \approx -6.708\,204
$$

rounded to six decimal places." :tutorial/id #uuid "5eb86849-2816-5e44-b2e4-786b170cf6d8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3274 :tutorial/title "Expressions Resulting in Radicals"} {:db/id 17592186079667 :tutorial/content "Suppose we need to evaluate an expression like

$$
1+\sqrt{4},
$$

where we have a square root sign. What would be the order of operations? It turns out that the root signs ($\sqrt{\phantom{x}}$ or $\sqrt[3]{\phantom{x}}$) can be thought of as parentheses. 
In other words, we find the value under the square root first:

$$
\begin{aligned}1+\sqrt{4} &= 1+2 \\ &= 3\end{aligned}
$$

 

Similarly, let's evaluate $\big(1-\sqrt[3]{-27}\big) \operatorname{div}  2$.

To evaluate expressions with radicals, we use PEMDAS as before, but with the following additional rules:

- expressions underneath radicals are treated the same as parentheses

- radicals themselves are treated as exponents

Following the order of operations, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}(1-\sqrt[3]{-27})÷2 &= (1-\sqrt[3]{(-3)^{3}})÷2 \\ &= (1-(-3))÷2 \\ &= 4÷2 \\ &= 2\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3d4a0de2-cecd-5c77-8bf2-40997a53ac9a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3292 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186079710 :tutorial/content "We know how to evaluate expressions like $2^3, 2^2, 2^1$, and even $2^0.$ But what if the power is negative? How would we evaluate $2^{-1},$ for example?

To help us with that, let's go back to the results table for powers of $2.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{4} & =16 \\ {2}^{3} & =8 \\ {2}^{2} & =4 \\ {2}^{1} & =2 \\ {2}^{0} & =1 \\ {2}^{-1} & =◻\,?\end{aligned}
$$

As we go down the list, the number in blue is divided by $2$ every time. If we follow the same pattern, we find that 

$$
2^{\color{red}{-1}} = {\color{blue}{1}}\operatorname{div}  2 = \dfrac{1}{2}.
$$

Now, $\dfrac{1}{2}$ is just the reciprocal of $2.$ So, raising a number to the power of $-1$ is the *same* as finding its reciprocal!" :tutorial/id #uuid "1a1e2f61-f43c-5311-914b-4898ea6cd4eb" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8016 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186082908 :question/id #uuid "150823b8-0a7b-54ac-97e0-32357764b648" :question/math-academy-id "e-11050" :question/problem "Given the sequences $a_n = \dfrac{1}{2n^2+n}$ and $b_n = \dfrac{1}{n^2}$, calculate $$
\displaystyle L = \lim_{n\to \infty} \dfrac{a_n}{b_n}
$$ and determine whether $$
\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n
$$ converges or diverges." :question/worked-solution "The limit comparison test states that if $a_n$ and $b_n$ are both positive, and

$$
\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \frac{a_n}{b_n} = L
$$

where $L$ is positive and finite, then the series

$$
\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n
$$

and

$$
\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n
$$

either *both* converge or *both* diverge.

The given series looks as though it will behave like the convergent series

$$
\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{1}{2n^2} = \dfrac 1 2\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{1}{n^2}
$$

So, we let

$$
a_n = \dfrac{1}{2n^2+n}, \qquad b_n = \dfrac{1}{n^2}
$$

Computing the limit of the ratio, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lim_{n \to  \infty}\frac{a_{n}}{b_{n}} &= \lim_{n \to  \infty}(\frac{1}{2n^{2} + n} \operatorname{div}  \frac{1}{n^{2}}) \\
&= \lim_{n \to  \infty}\left(\frac{n^{2}}{2n^{2} + n}\right) \\
&= \lim_{n \to  \infty}(1)/((2 + \frac{1}{n})) \\
&= \frac{1}{2 + 0} \\
&= \frac{1}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $a_n$ and $b_n$ are both positive and

$$
\displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \frac{a_n}{b_n} = \dfrac12
$$

is positive and finite, we can use the limit comparison test.

So, since

$$
\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n
$$

converges, then

$$
\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n
$$

converges as well. Therefore, the series

$$
\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{1}{2n^2+n}
$$

converges."} {:db/id 17592186082909 :question/id #uuid "ae0269fe-a9d9-5582-8b9d-e6841c405278" :question/math-academy-id "e-11051" :question/problem "Given the sequences $a_n = \dfrac{2n^3-n^2}{4n^4+n}$ and $b_n = \dfrac{1}{n}$, calculate $$
\displaystyle L = \lim_{n\to\infty}\dfrac{a_n}{b_n}
$$ and determine whether $$
\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n
$$ converges or diverges." :question/worked-solution "The limit comparison test states that if $a_n$ and $b_n$ are both positive, and

$$
\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \frac{a_n}{b_n} = L
$$

where $L$ is positive and finite, then the series

$$
\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n
$$

and

$$
\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n
$$

either *both* converge or *both* diverge.

The given series looks as though it will behave like the divergent series

$$
\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{2n^3}{4n^4} = \dfrac 2 4\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{n^3}{n^4} = \dfrac 1 2\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{1}{n}
$$

So, we let

$$
a_n = \dfrac{2n^3 - n^2}{4n^4+n}, \qquad b_n = \dfrac{1}{n}
$$

Computing the limit of the ratio, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lim_{n \to  \infty}\frac{a_{n}}{b_{n}} &= \lim_{n \to  \infty}(\frac{2n^{3} - n^{2}}{4n^{4} + n} \operatorname{div}  \frac{1}{n}) \\
&= \lim_{n \to  \infty}(\frac{2n^{3} - n^{2}}{4n^{4} + n} \cdot n) \\
&= \lim_{n \to  \infty}\left(\frac{2n^{4} - n^{3}}{4n^{4} + n}\right) \\
&= \lim_{n \to  \infty}(((2 - \frac{1}{n}))/((4 + \frac{1}{n^{3}}))) \\
&= \frac{2 - 0}{4 + 0} \\
&= \frac{1}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $a_n$ and $b_n$ are both positive, and

$$
\displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \frac{a_n}{b_n} = \dfrac{1}{2}
$$

is positive and finite, we can use the limit comparison test.

So, since

$$
\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n
$$

diverges, then

$$
\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n
$$

diverges as well. Therefore, the series

$$
\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{2n^3-n^2}{4n^4+n}
$$

diverges."} {:db/id 17592186082910 :question/id #uuid "78026037-a204-5416-8401-5a68adbc5f4e" :question/math-academy-id "e-11052" :question/problem "Given the sequences $a_n = \dfrac{3(2^n)+1}{2(3^n)+1}$ and $b_n = \left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^n$, calculate $$
\displaystyle L = \lim_{n\to\infty}\dfrac{a_n}{b_n}
$$ and determine whether $$
\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n
$$ converges or diverges." :question/worked-solution "The limit comparison test states that if $a_n$ and $b_n$ are both positive, and

$$
\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \frac{a_n}{b_n} = L
$$

where $L$ is positive and finite, then the series

$$
\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n
$$

and

$$
\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n
$$

either *both* converge or *both* diverge.

The given series looks as though it will behave like the convergent geometric series

$$
\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{2^n}{3^n} = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \left(\dfrac{2}{3} \right)^n
$$

We know the above series converges because it is a geometric series with common ratio

$$
\mid r \mid = \dfrac{2}{3} < 1
$$

So, we let

$$
a_n = \dfrac{3(2^n)+1}{2(3^n)+1}, \qquad b_n = \left(\dfrac{2}{3} \right)^n
$$

Computing the limit of the ratio, we get

$$
{\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle \lim_{n \to  \mathrm{\infty }} {\displaystyle \frac{ {a}_{n}}{ {b}_{n}}} & \displaystyle  = \lim_{n \to  \mathrm{\infty }} ( {\displaystyle \frac{3 ( {2}^{n} ) + 1}{2 ( {3}^{n} ) + 1}} \operatorname{div}   {\displaystyle \frac{ {2}^{n}}{ {3}^{n}}} ) \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = \lim_{n \to  \mathrm{\infty }} ( {\displaystyle \frac{3 ( {2}^{n} ) + 1}{2 ( {3}^{n} ) + 1}} \cdot  {\displaystyle \frac{ {3}^{n}}{ {2}^{n}}} ) \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = \lim_{n \to  \mathrm{\infty }} ( {\displaystyle \frac{ {2}^{n} ( 3 + {2}^{- n} )}{ {3}^{n} ( 2 + {3}^{- n} )}} \cdot  {\displaystyle \frac{ {3}^{n}}{ {2}^{n}}} ) \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = \lim_{n \to  \mathrm{\infty }} ( {\displaystyle \frac{\cancel{ {2}^{n}} ( 3 + {2}^{- n} )}{\cancel{ {3}^{n}} ( 2 + {3}^{- n} )}} \cdot  {\displaystyle \frac{\cancel{ {3}^{n}}}{\cancel{ {2}^{n}}}} ) \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = \lim_{n \to  \mathrm{\infty }} ( {\displaystyle \frac{3 + {2}^{- n}}{2 + {3}^{- n}}} ) \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{3 + 2 ( 0 )}{2 + 3 ( 0 )}} \\ \displaystyle  & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{3}{2}} .\end{array}}
$$

Since $a_n$ and $b_n$ are both positive and

$$
\displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \frac{a_n}{b_n} = \dfrac{3}{2}
$$

is positive and finite, we can use the limit comparison test.

So, since

$$
\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n
$$

converges, then

$$
\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n
$$

converges as well. Therefore, the series

$$
\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{3(2^n)+1}{2(3^n)+1}
$$

converges."} {:db/id 17592186082911 :question/id #uuid "cb71010d-2ba3-531b-846b-0de4b5f6de74" :question/math-academy-id "e-11053" :question/problem "Given the sequences $a_n = \dfrac{\sqrt[3]{n^2}}{3n+4}$ and $b_n = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$, calculate $$
\displaystyle L = \lim_{n\to\infty}\dfrac{a_n}{b_n}
$$ and determine whether $$
\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n
$$ converges or diverges." :question/worked-solution "Let $a_n$ and $b_n$ be two positive sequences. The one-sided limit comparison tests state the following:

- If $$
\displaystyle \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \frac{a_n}{b_n} = 0,
$$ and it is known that $$
\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n
$$ converges, then $$
\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n
$$ also converges.
- If $$
\displaystyle \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \frac{a_n}{b_n} = \infty,
$$ and it is known that $$
\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n
$$ diverges, then $$
\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n
$$ also diverges.

First, notice that

$$
\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n
$$

is a divergent $p$-series.

Computing the limit of the ratio, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
L &= \lim_{n \to  \infty}\frac{a_{n}}{b_{n}} \\
&= \lim_{n \to  \infty}(\frac{\sqrt[3]{n^{2}}}{3n + 4} \operatorname{div}  \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}) \\
&= \lim_{n \to  \infty}(\frac{\sqrt[3]{n^{2}}}{3n + 4} \cdot \sqrt{n}) \\
&= \lim_{n \to  \infty}(\frac{n^{2/3}}{3n + 4} \cdot n^{1/2}) \\
&= \lim_{n \to  \infty}\left(\frac{n^{7/6}}{3n + 4}\right) \\
&= \lim_{n \to  \infty}\left(\frac{n^{1/6}}{3 + 4/n}\right) \\
&= \frac{∞}{3 + 0} \\
&= ∞
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $a_n$ and $b_n$ are both positive and

$$
\lim\limits_{n \to\infty} \dfrac{a_n}{b_n}=\infty
$$

we can use the one-sided comparison test.

So, since

$$
\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n
$$

diverges, then

$$
\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n
$$

diverges as well. Therefore, the series

$$
\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{\sqrt[3]{n^2}}{3n+4}
$$

diverges."} {:db/id 17592186082950 :question/id #uuid "f1285d13-fbc3-5803-b895-cb1b3b930089" :question/math-academy-id "e-1495" :question/problem "A company manufactures teddy bears. The revenue and cost functions, in thousands of dollars, of this company are given by

$$
\displaystyle C(x) = 6\,700 + 26x, \qquad R(x) = 130x - 0.4x^2,
$$

where $x$ represents the number of units produced per month. Find the number of units the company should produce per month to make a profit of $\$20\,000$." :question/worked-solution "The profit is equal to the revenue minus the cost:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(x) &= R(x) - C(x) \\
&= (130x - 0.4x^{2}) - (6700 + 26x) \\
&=-0.4x^{2} + 104x - 6700
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since we want a profit of $\$20\,000$, and $P(x)$ is measured in thousands of dollars, we set $P(x)$ equal to

$$
20\,000\operatorname{div}  1\,000 = 20
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(x) &= 20 \\
- 0.4x^{2} + 104x - 6700 &= 20
\end{aligned}
$$

We can tidy up the equation so that it becomes a quadratic equation in standard form with a leading coefficient of $1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
-0.4x^{2} + 104x - 6700 &= 20 \\
0.4x^{2} - 104x + 6720 &= 0 \\
\frac{0.4x^{2} - 104x + 6720}{0.4} &= \frac{0}{0.4} \\
x^{2} - 260x + 16800 &= 0
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to solve for $x$, we apply the quadratic formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= (- (-260) ± \sqrt{(-260)^{2} - 4(1)(16800)})/(2) \\
&= \frac{260 ± \sqrt{400}}{2} \\
&= \frac{260 ± 20}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions are $x=120$ and $x=140$. Therefore, the company will make a profit of $\$20\,000$ if it produces $120$ or $140$ units."} {:db/id 17592186083097 :question/id #uuid "546e8fe6-d487-5baf-bf40-7fbdd59191bb" :question/math-academy-id "e-714" :question/problem "Use the ratio test to show that $$
\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{n}{3^n}
$$ is convergent." :question/worked-solution "Let

$$
a_n = \dfrac{n}{3^n}
$$

If we replace $n$ with $n+1$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned} a_{n+1}= \frac{n+1}{3^{n+1}}= \frac{n+1}{3\cdot 3^n}. \end{aligned}
$$

Now that we have expressions for the consecutive terms $a_n$ and $a_{n+1}$, we can work out the necessary limit:

$$
\begin{aligned} L &=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \right| \\[5pt] &=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\frac{n+1}{3\cdot 3^n} \operatorname{div}  \frac{n}{3^n}\right) \\[5pt] &= \lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\frac{n+1}{3\cdot 3^n} \cdot \frac{3^n}{n}\right) \\[5pt] &= \lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\frac{n+1}{3n} \right) \\[5pt] &= \lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{n+1}{n}\right) \\[5pt] &= \frac{1}{3}\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(1 + \frac{1}{n}\right) \\[5pt] &=\frac{1}{3}\left(1 + 0\right) \\[5pt] &=\frac{1}{3}. \end{aligned}
$$

Note that we dropped the absolute value bars because the sequence is positive for all

$$
n\geq 1
$$

Since

$$
L = \dfrac{1}{3}<1
$$

we conclude that the series is convergent by the ratio test."} {:db/id 17592186083098 :question/id #uuid "18893844-6e54-5acc-b975-2755fcb31a04" :question/math-academy-id "e-715" :question/problem "Use the ratio test to show that $$
\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n\, n!}{3^n}
$$ is divergent." :question/worked-solution "This is an example of an **alternating series**. The $(-1)^n$ causes the signs of the successive terms to alternate between positive and negative.

Let

$$
a_n = \dfrac{(-1)^n\,n!}{3^n}
$$

If we replace $n$ with $n+1$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned} a_{n+1}= \dfrac{(-1)^{n+1}(n+1)!}{3^{n+1}}= \frac{(-1)^{n+1}\,(n+1)!}{3\cdot 3^n}. \end{aligned}
$$

Now that we have expressions for the consecutive terms $a_n$ and $a_{n+1}$, we can work out the necessary limit:

$$
\begin{aligned} L &=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \right| \\[5pt] &=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left| \dfrac{(-1)^{n+1}\,(n+1)!}{3\cdot 3^n} \operatorname{div}  \dfrac{(-1)^n\,n!}{3^n}\right| \\[5pt] &=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left| \dfrac{(-1)^{n+1}\,(n+1)!}{3\cdot 3^n} \cdot \dfrac{3^n}{(-1)^n\,n!}\right| \\[5pt] &=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left|-\dfrac{n+1}{3}\right| \\[5pt] &=\dfrac 1 3\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(n+1\right) \\[5pt] &=\infty. \end{aligned}
$$

Since

$$
L=\infty > 1
$$

we conclude that the series is divergent by the ratio test."} {:db/id 17592186083099 :question/id #uuid "2fa6106f-193b-5aa2-ad19-2cb4833e7e2f" :question/math-academy-id "e-716" :question/problem "Use the ratio test to determine whether the series $$
\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{2n+1}
$$ is convergent or divergent." :question/worked-solution "Let

$$
a_n = \dfrac{1}{2n+1}
$$

If we replace $n$ with $n+1$, we get

$$
a_{n+1} = \frac{1}{2(n+1)+1}= \frac{1}{2n+3}
$$

Now that we have expressions for the consecutive terms $a_n$ and $a_{n+1}$, we can work out the necessary limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}
L &= \lim_{n \to  \infty} \mid \frac{a_{n + 1}}{a_{n}} \mid \\
&= \lim_{n \to  \infty} \mid \frac{a_{n + 1}}{a_{n}} \mid \\
&= \lim_{n \to  \infty} \mid \frac{1}{2n + 3} \operatorname{div}  \frac{1}{2n + 1} \mid \\
&= \lim_{n \to  \infty}(\frac{1}{2n + 3} \cdot \frac{2n + 1}{1}) \\
&= \lim_{n \to  \infty}\left(\frac{2n + 1}{2n + 3}\right) \\
&= \lim_{n \to  \infty}\left(\frac{2 + \frac{1}{n}}{2 + \frac{3}{n}}\right) \\
&= \frac{2}{2} \\
&= 1
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $L=1$, the ratio test gives *no conclusion* about whether the series is convergent or divergent.

**Note:** Although the ratio test gave no conclusion, the series

$$
\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{2n+1}
$$

is actually divergent."} {:db/id 17592186084503 :tutorial/content "Let's use the limit comparison test to determine whether the following series converges or diverges:

$$
\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{1}{n + 2}
$$

This looks a bit like the diverging $p$-series

$$
\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{1}{n}
$$

However, we cannot use the comparison test because

$$
\dfrac{1}{n + 2} < \dfrac{1}{n}
$$

Let's instead try the limit comparison test. Let

$$
a_n = \dfrac{1}{n + 2}, \qquad b_n = \dfrac{1}{n}
$$

Computing the limit of the ratio, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lim_{n \to  \infty}\frac{a_{n}}{b_{n}} &= \lim_{n \to  \infty}\frac{1}{n + 2} \operatorname{div}  \frac{1}{n} \\
&= \lim_{n \to  \infty}\frac{n}{n + 2} \\
&= \lim_{n \to  \infty}(\left(\frac{n}{n}\right))/((\frac{n}{n} + \frac{2}{n})) \\
&= \lim_{n \to  \infty}(1)/((1 + \frac{2}{n})) \\
&= \frac{1}{1 + 0} \\
&= 1
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $a_n$ and $b_n$ are both positive and

$$
\displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \frac{a_n}{b_n} = 1
$$

is positive and finite, we can use the limit comparison test.

So, since

$$
\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n
$$

diverges, then

$$
\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n
$$

diverges as well. Therefore, the series

$$
\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{1}{n + 2}
$$

diverges." :tutorial/id #uuid "fe6f3ca2-0727-55ef-861a-0d70b5fa96ef" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7658 :tutorial/title "A Concrete Example"} {:db/id 17592186087429 :question/id #uuid "1888cff7-d547-587d-bc00-33cbde777370" :question/math-academy-id "e-12670" :question/problem "Which of the following numbers are **prime factors** of $12$?

1. $3$
2. $4$
3. $5$" :question/worked-solution "The prime factors of a number are the primes that divide the number with no remainder.

The first few prime numbers are given below.

$$
2, \quad 3, \quad 5, \quad 7, \quad 11, \quad \ldots
$$

Let's see which of the given numbers are prime factors of $12{:}$

- $3$ is prime. Also, $3$ is a factor of $12$ since $12 \operatorname{div}  3 = 4. \quad \color{green} \checkmark$
- $4$ is **not** prime.

- $5$ is prime. However, $5$ is **not** a factor of $12$ since dividing $12$ by
$5$ gives a remainder of $2.\quad\color{red} \times$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$3$ only.""} {:db/id 17592186088988 :tutorial/content "The first few prime numbers are

$$
2,\quad 3, \quad 5, \quad 7, \quad 11, \quad 13, \quad 17, \quad 19, \quad 23, \quad 29, \quad \ldots\,.
$$

Remember that $1$ is *not* a prime number.

A number's **prime factors** are the prime numbers that divide the number with no remainder. 

Let's list the prime factors of $45{:}$

- $2$ is *not* a prime factor of $45$ since dividing $45$ by $2$ gives a remainder of $1. \quad{\color{red}{\times}}$

- $3$ *is* a prime factor of $45$ since $45 \operatorname{div}  3 = 15.\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}$

- $5$ *is* a prime factor of $45$ since $45 \operatorname{div}  5 = 9.\quad{\color{green}{\checkmark}}$

- $7$ is *not* a prime factor of $45$ since dividing $45$ by $7$ gives a remainder of $3. \quad{\color{red}{\times}}$

There are no other prime numbers that divide $45.$ Therefore, the prime factors of $45$ are $3$ and $5.$

We often wish to find a number's prime factors. We'll discuss this more in a future lesson." :tutorial/id #uuid "de204ea3-c1d3-5d64-979c-a9285f3da4ca" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7959 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186091946 :question/id #uuid "5ae8b304-5ce3-5520-8893-92a02784155d" :question/math-academy-id "e-1316" :question/problem "Which of the following expressions are polynomials?

I. $(5x^2-10x^3) \operatorname{div}  (5x)$

II. $(1-x^3) \operatorname{div}  (x^3)$

III. $(2x^5) \cdot (-x^3-7)$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that polynomials have the following closure properties:

- Polynomials are closed under addition, subtraction, and multiplication. This means that the sum, difference, and product of two polynomials is *always* a polynomial.

- Polynomials are *not* closed under division. This means that the quotient of two polynomials is *not* always a polynomial.

With that in mind, let's examine our expressions in turn.

- Expression I is a polynomial. Even though polynomials are *not* closed under division, the quotient of these two polynomials results in a polynomial:

$$
\begin{aligned}(5{x}^{2}-10{x}^{3})÷(5x) & =\frac{5{x}^{2}-10{x}^{3}}{5x} \\  & =\frac{5x(x-2{x}^{2})}{5x} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{5x}(x-2{x}^{2})}{\cancel{5x}} \\  & =x-2{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- Expression II is *not* a polynomial. Carrying out the division, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1-{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}} & =\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}-1\end{aligned}
$$

which is *not* a polynomial.

- Expression III is a polynomial. It's a product of two polynomials, and polynomials are closed under multiplication.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only.""} {:db/id 17592186092554 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "d0210349-d658-56bd-8f80-e31fccac3a60" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/id 17592186089496} {:answer/id #uuid "e1eb60db-f954-5877-a166-eaa4edacda1b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186089497} {:answer/id #uuid "0f0c2601-d71d-5e69-8744-62171093b7de" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186089498} {:answer/id #uuid "2f9c787c-b254-506e-a140-14df70ac0529" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186089499} {:answer/id #uuid "39bbda71-17a5-5873-b28b-20983276c6e9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186089500}] :answer-field/id #uuid "0f0b6a73-9b4a-5a58-b5c8-ca19e491d602" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186089495}] :question/id #uuid "f96cf055-993b-5aae-b24a-69010655c966" :question/math-academy-id "q-141204" :question/problem "Which of the following expressions are polynomials?

1. $(-7x) + (2x^{2} + x)$
2. $(2x - x^{3}) \operatorname{div}  (x)$
3. $(2x^{7}) \cdot (1 + 2x^{5})$"} {:db/id 17592186100600 :question/id #uuid "20a3ff12-b7fa-590f-a32e-c2b922324a3d" :question/math-academy-id "e-13042" :question/problem "Express $\dfrac{(-5)^{7}}{(-5)^3}$ as a base raised to a single exponent." :question/worked-solution "First, we write the fraction as a division:

$$
\dfrac{(-5)^{7}}{(-5)^3} = (-5)^{7} \operatorname{div}  (-5)^3
$$

Now, to divide powers of the same base, we simply subtract the exponents:

$$
(-5)^{7} \operatorname{div}  (-5)^3 = (-5)^{7-3} = (-5)^{4}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186100601 :question/id #uuid "482947e3-a48c-5196-b46c-29aa03ddb57e" :question/math-academy-id "e-13043" :question/problem "Express $$
\displaystyle \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^4 \operatorname{div}  \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2
$$ as a base raised to a single exponent." :question/worked-solution "To divide powers of the same base, we simply subtract the exponents:

$$
\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^4 \operatorname{div}  \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{4-2}= \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186100602 :question/id #uuid "3c2c32f1-4e6d-5363-9145-5834c59e7fd9" :question/math-academy-id "e-13044" :question/problem "Express $\dfrac{0.2^5}{0.2^2}$ as a base raised to a single exponent." :question/worked-solution "First, we write the fraction as a division:

$$
\dfrac{0.2^5}{0.2^2} = 0.2^5 \operatorname{div}  0.2^2
$$

Now, to divide powers of the same base, we simply subtract the exponents:

$$
\begin{aligned}{0.2}^{5}÷{0.2}^{2}={0.2}^{5-2}={0.2}^{3}\end{aligned}

:question/math-academy-id "q-68358" :question/problem "What is $3^{-5} \operatorname{div}  3^{-2}$?"} {:db/id 17592186102023 :tutorial/content "To divide powers of the same base, we simply *subtract* the exponents. This is known as the **quotient rule for exponents**. For instance, in the expression 

$$
{\color{blue}3}^5 \operatorname{div}  {\color{blue}3}^2,
$$

both powers have the same base $({\color{blue}3})$. Therefore, we can simplify this expression by subtracting the exponents:

$$
{\color{blue}3}^5 \operatorname{div}  {\color{blue}3}^2 = {\color{blue}3}^{5-2} = {\color{blue}3}^3.
$$

**Note:** The quotient rule for exponents is really just a quicker alternative to the following process:

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{5}÷{3}^{2} &= {3}^{3+2}÷{3}^{2} \\ &= {3}^{3}\times \underbrace{{3}^{2}÷{3}^{2}}_{=1} \\ &= {3}^{3}\times 1 \\ &= {3}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "4547d33f-6904-539f-b917-599af56aac3b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8158 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186102024 :tutorial/content "We can use the quotient rule for exponents with negative exponents too. For example, to simplify $3^{-5}\operatorname{div}  3^{-3},$ we subtract the exponents:

$$
3^{-5} \operatorname{div}  3^{-3} = 3^{-5-(-3)} = 3^{-2}
$$

Now, to evaluate $3^{-2},$ we find the reciprocal of the base $(3)$ and then raise that reciprocal to the same power but with the opposite sign:

$$
3^{-2}  = \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^2 =\dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{1}{9}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b127450f-67ae-5232-a082-2242758636fd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8160 :tutorial/title "The Quotient Rule With Negative Exponents"} {:answer/id #uuid "b358e447-f1de-5dec-828f-1655ba8181dd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4 \operatorname{div}  (11 \cdot 3)" :db/id 17592186104963} {:answer/id #uuid "d299947e-3567-54b1-a03a-3c24f5b92fbf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4^{3} \operatorname{div}  11" :db/id 17592186104964} {:answer/id #uuid "f2351657-92f5-5246-8ba3-edb15734d2ea" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4 \operatorname{div}  (11 + 3)" :db/id 17592186104965} {:answer/id #uuid "18d1c353-4eb5-54c8-b659-08b5f9054710" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4^{3} \operatorname{div}  11^{3}" :db/id 17592186104966} {:answer/id #uuid "53fb43f0-05c0-595d-92b8-4e2380d39a38" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4 \operatorname{div}  11^{3}" :db/id 17592186104967} {:db/id 17592186114997 :question/id #uuid "ea4a1d2b-d7d7-5da8-8750-87e6ab887b1a" :question/math-academy-id "e-3311" :question/problem "The area of the circular sector shown below is $6\pi\,\textrm{m}^2$. If the measure of the central angle corresponding to the major arc is $\dfrac{4}{3}\pi$ radians, what is the radius of the circle?

![](images/2c/2c0a19b4890c1f0e3aa2bef49176a07f597da2be8684e7efe3491fafd528d269.png)" :question/worked-solution "Here, we are given that the area of the sector is

$$
\mathcal{A}=6\pi\,\textrm{m}^2
$$

and the central angle is

$$
\theta=\dfrac{4}{3}\pi
$$

radians.

Rearranging the formula for the area of a sector, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
A &= \frac{r^{2}θ}{2} \\
r^{2}θ &= 2A \\
r^{2} &= \frac{2A}{θ}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
r^{2} &= \frac{2 \cdot A}{θ} \\
&= (2 \cdot 6π)/((\frac{4}{3}π)) \\
&= 12π \operatorname{div}  \frac{4π}{3} \\
&= 12π \cdot \frac{3}{4π} \\
&= \frac{36π}{4π} \\
&= 9
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
r=\sqrt{9} = 3\,\textrm{m}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186119493 :question/id #uuid "aa638025-6c2e-53fe-a1b8-77a6ba49bf66" :question/math-academy-id "e-10119" :question/problem "Evaluate $\dfrac{e+7}{\pi-1}$." :question/worked-solution "Recall that we always round to $3$ decimal places unless stated otherwise.

Our expression can be written as follows:

$$
\dfrac{e+7}{\pi-1} = {\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{(}e+7\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{)}} \operatorname{div}  {\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{(}\pi-1\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{)}}
$$

We're now ready to enter this expression into a calculator. To do so, we note the following:

- We enter the symbols from left to right as they appear.
- Your calculator will have special $\bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,(\,}$ and $\bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,)\,}$ buttons for left and right parentheses.
- Scientific and graphing calculators usually have special $\bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,e\,}$ and $\bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\pi\,}$ buttons. You may need to press $\bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\textrm{2nd}}$ or $\bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\textrm{SHIFT}}$ to access these.

Notice the parentheses in the expression above.

Evaluating this using a calculator, we obtain

$$
(e+7) \operatorname{div}  (\pi-1) \approx 4.538
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186119507 :question/id #uuid "ae97ecae-5372-59f9-9626-a62c17094a4b" :question/math-academy-id "e-1207" :question/problem "Consider the relationship between $x$ and $y$ shown below.

2. The relationship between $x$ and $y$ is exponential
3. If $x$ is increased by $1$, then $y$ increases by a factor of $10$" :question/worked-solution "To determine if the relationship is linear or exponential, we need to determine how $y$ changes as $x$ increases at each step:

- For a linear relationship, there should be a common *difference* between successive values of $y$.
- For an exponential relationship, there should be a common *ratio* between successive values of $y$.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement.

- Statement I is false, while statement II is true. Let's check for a common ratio by dividing successive values of $y$. We see that
$1 \operatorname{div}  \left(\dfrac15\right) = 5$,
and similarly,
$$
\displaystyle \frac{5}{1} = \frac{25}{5} = 5.
$$
Since the *ratio* of any two successive terms is constant, the relationship is *exponential*. In this case, the common ratio is $5$.
- Statement III is false. When $x$ increases by $1$, the respective value of $y$ increases by a factor of $5$, not $10$.

$$
\dfrac{\pi}{e-1}
$$

Using parentheses when inputting the denominator $e-1$ into a calculator is *essential*. This is because $\pi \operatorname{div}  e - 1$ is equivalent to 

$$
\dfrac{\pi}e - 1
$$

 
which is *not* the same as the expression we want to evaluate! 

So, let's begin by rewriting our expression using parentheses:

$$
\dfrac{\pi}{e-1} = \pi \operatorname{div}  \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{(}e - 1\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{)}
$$

We're now ready to enter this expression into a calculator. To do so, we note the following:

- We enter the symbols from left to right as they appear.

- Your calculator will have special $\bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,(\,}$ and $\bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,)\,}$ buttons for left and right parentheses.

- Scientific and graphing calculators usually have special $\bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,e\,}$ and $\bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\pi\,}$ buttons. You may need to press $\bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\textrm{2nd}}$ or $\bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\textrm{SHIFT}}$ to access these.

Evaluating this using a calculator, we obtain

$$
\pi \operatorname{div}  (e - 1) \approx 1.828
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

When evaluating expressions on a scientific or graphing calculator, we always round to $3$ decimal places unless stated otherwise." :tutorial/id #uuid "e46b9c13-e921-5dd5-9174-73d35ca35f9e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6306 :tutorial/title "Evaluating an Expression Using a Calculator"} {:db/id 17592186121118 :tutorial/content "Most calculators have a special $\bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\sqrt{\phantom{0}}\,}$ button for the square root. However, many calculators do not have a special symbol for other radicals.

If your calculator *does* have a button for other radicals, it will look similar to $\bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\sqrt[n]{x}\,}.$ 

An alternative way to compute the numerical value of a radical is to rewrite the expression as a fractional exponent and then use the exponent button. Common symbols used for the exponent button are $\bbox[5px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\land\,},$ $\bbox[5px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,x^y\,},$ or similar.

Let's use the exponent button to evaluate the following expression to $5$ decimal places:

$$
\sqrt[7]{38}
$$

Firstly, our radical can be written as a fractional exponent as follows:

$$
\sqrt[7]{38} = 38^{\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{1/7}}
$$

So, we'd use a sequence of buttons similar to the following to evaluate this expression:

$$
\bbox[6px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,3\,}  \qquad
\bbox[6px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,8\,}  \qquad
\bbox[6px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\land\,} \qquad
\bbox[6px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,1\,}  \qquad
\bbox[5px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\operatorname{div} \,}  \qquad
\bbox[7px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,7\,}
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
38^{1/7} \approx 1.681\,45
$$

rounded to $5$ decimal places.

**Watch out!** In the sequence of buttons above, we assume that pressing the exponent button moves the cursor upwards into a superscript. If your calculator does not do this, then it is likely necessary to enclose the exponent in parentheses:

$$
\bbox[6px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,3\,}  \qquad
\bbox[6px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,8\,}  \qquad
\bbox[6px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\land\,} \qquad
\bbox[6px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,(\,}  \qquad
\bbox[6px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,1\,}  \qquad
\bbox[5px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\operatorname{div} \,}  \qquad
\bbox[7px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,7\,} \qquad
\bbox[6px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,)\,}  \qquad
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "beab0b65-7a4a-5dda-acb9-dd9b3b44aa50" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6308 :tutorial/title "Evaluating Radicals"} {:db/id 17592186128870 :question/id #uuid "e2f973d4-5d1e-5e35-84d3-277d1069d6f7" :question/math-academy-id "e-12873" :question/problem "Calculate $10\operatorname{div}  5^0 + (3^2-5).$" :question/worked-solution "To evaluate the given expression, we use PEMDAS.

First, we compute the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}10÷{5}^{0}+(9-5)=10÷{5}^{0}+4\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that $5^0=1.$ So, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}10÷{5}^{0}+4 &= 10÷1+4 \\ &= 10+4 \\ &= 14\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186128872 :question/id #uuid "c6b6a911-843f-5c96-a792-ebd807b5d60e" :question/math-academy-id "e-12875" :question/problem "Find the value of $2 + \left(-4\right)^{-2} \operatorname{div}  \left( 1.5 + \dfrac{2}{15} \right)^0.$" :question/worked-solution "To evaluate the given expression, we use PEMDAS.

Any number raised to the power of $0$ equals $1.$ So, we have 

$$
\left( 1.5 + \dfrac{2}{15} \right) ^0 = 1.
$$

Next, we evaluate the negative exponent and get

$$
\left(-4\right)^{-2}  = \dfrac{1}{(-4)^2} = \dfrac{1}{16}.
$$

Substituting all these values into the expression, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}2+{(-4)}^{-2}÷{(1.5+\frac{2}{15})}^{0} &= 2+\frac{1}{16}÷1 \\ &= 2+\frac{1}{16} \\ &= \frac{32}{16}+\frac{1}{16} \\ &= \frac{33}{16}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129400 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c1dc5959-afee-5ebf-ab0a-11fb12b562ef" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id "Rational expressions are *closed* under the arithmetic operations of addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division.

So, we have that:

- The *sum* of two rational expressions is a rational expression:
$\textrm{rational} + \textrm{rational} = \textrm{rational}$
- The *difference* between two rational expressions is a rational expression:
$\textrm{rational} - \textrm{rational} = \textrm{rational}$
- The *product* of two rational expressions is a rational expression:
$\textrm{rational} \:\cdot\: \textrm{rational} = \textrm{rational}$
- The *quotient* of two rational expressions is a rational expression:
$\textrm{rational} \operatorname{div}  \textrm{rational} = \textrm{rational}$
provided that the denominator is nonzero.

In this sense, rational expressions and rational numbers have similar properties." :tutorial/id #uuid "0e3a486b-3804-5128-a6b4-9865034f8c9b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6059 :tutorial/title "Closure Properties of Rational Expressions"} {:db/id 17592186130481 :tutorial/content "As we know already, to evaluate numerical expressions with a mix of different operations, we follow the order of operations (PEMDAS).

The same rules apply to numerical expressions with zero and negative exponents. To demonstrate, let's compute the value of

$$
(-3)^0 +2^2 \operatorname{div}  2.
$$

To evaluate the given expression, we use PEMDAS.

Notice that $\left(-3\right)^{0}=1.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{(-3)}^{0}+{2}^{2}÷2 &= 1+{2}^{2}÷2 \\ &= 1+4÷2 \\ &= 1+2 \\ &= 3.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e2d29fa0-8bcb-537b-bed9-91a9ff109764" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8061 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186133496 :question/id #uuid "fc3055a3-5118-5a5b-8150-caadbfdae02b" :question/math-academy-id "e-12788" :question/problem "What is the reciprocal of $-21?$" :question/worked-solution "To find the reciprocal of $-21,$ we divide $1$ by $-21.$ So, we obtain 

$$
1 \operatorname{div}  (-21) = -\dfrac{1}{21}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186135172 :tutorial/content "The **reciprocal** of a number is equal to ${\color{red}{1}}$ divided by the number. For example:

- the reciprocal of ${\color{blue}{2}}$ is equal to ${\color{red}{1}} \operatorname{div}  {\color{blue}{2}} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

- the reciprocal of ${\color{blue}{3}}$ is equal to  ${\color{red}{1}} \operatorname{div}  {\color{blue}{3}} = \dfrac{1}{3}$

- the reciprocal of $-{\color{blue}{7}}$ is equal to  ${\color{red}{1}} \operatorname{div}  ({\color{blue}{-7}}) = -\dfrac{1}{7}$

The reciprocal of ${\color{blue}{1}}$ is  equal to  ${\color{red}{1}} \operatorname{div}  {\color{blue}{1}} = 1.$ So the number $1$ is equal to its reciprocal. The same is true for $-1.$

The reciprocal of a number always has the same sign as the original number.

- If the number is positive, its reciprocal will be positive, while

- if the number is negative, its reciprocal is also negative." :tutorial/id #uuid "bcbb31e1-711c-5521-b35a-8fe1e56f4b95" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8017 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186138086 :question/id #uuid "c70c6338-9fcf-5672-a5f5-47ff0c8a2bf4" :question/math-academy-id "e-13470" :question/problem "Find the value of $2\,\dfrac 5 {10} + 4\,\dfrac 3 {10}$." :question/worked-solution "To add two mixed numbers, we add

- whole numbers to whole numbers, and
- fractions to fractions.

With that in mind let's add our mixed numbers.

- Adding the whole numbers, we get
$2 + 4 = {\color{red}{6}}$.
- Adding the fractions, we get
$$
\displaystyle \dfrac 5 {10} + \dfrac 3 {10} = \dfrac{5+3}{10} = \dfrac 8 {10}.
$$
We can simplify this fraction by dividing the numerator and denominator by $2{:}$
$$
\displaystyle \dfrac{8}{10} = \dfrac{8\operatorname{div}  2}{10\operatorname{div}  2} = {\color{blue}{\dfrac{4}{5}}}
$$

Therefore,

$$
2\,\dfrac 5 {10} + 4\,\dfrac 3 {10} = {\color{red}{6}} + {\color{blue}{\dfrac 4 5}} = 6\,\dfrac 4 5
$$"} {:db/id 17592186138091 :question/id #uuid "be7e80d2-601c-5320-9aa0-f017331c5607" :question/math-academy-id "e-13500" :question/problem "Which mixed number is equivalent to $51.4$?" :question/worked-solution "Whenever we write a decimal as a mixed number, our mixed number will have

- a *whole number part* that corresponds to the whole number to the left of the decimal point, and
- a *fractional part* that corresponds to the decimal part to the right of the decimal point.

With that in mind, let's write ${\color{blue}51}.\!{\color{red}4}$ as a mixed number.

- The whole number part is ${\color{blue}51}$.
- The decimal part has $1$ decimal place, so we can write it as a fraction in the following way:
$0.4= \dfrac{4}{10}$
Now we reduce the fraction to its simplest form by dividing the numerator and denominator by $2{:}$
$$
\displaystyle \dfrac{4}{10} = \dfrac{4 \operatorname{div}  2}{10 \operatorname{div}  2} = {\color{red}\dfrac{2}{5}}
$$

Therefore, we can write the given decimal as the following mixed number:

$$
51.4 = 51 \, \dfrac{2}{5}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186138100 :question/id #uuid "105a0a49-ea48-51f8-961d-269ec910b94c" :question/math-academy-id "e-13550" :question/problem "What mixed number is equivalent to $\dfrac{71}{8}$?" :question/worked-solution "First, we divide $71$ by ${\color{blue}{8}}{:}$

$$
71 \operatorname{div}  8 = 8\, \textrm{R}\,{\color{red}{7}}
$$

So, our division gives $8$ wholes, and we're left with

$$
\dfrac{\color{red}7}{\color{blue}8}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\dfrac{71}{8} = 8\,\dfrac{\color{red}7}{\color{blue}8}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186138101 :question/id #uuid "3ba209c9-cae2-5c20-86f4-44c571c223f2" :question/math-academy-id "e-13551" :question/problem "Find a mixed number equivalent to $\dfrac{51}{6}$." :question/worked-solution "First, we divide $51$ by ${\color{blue}{6}}{:}$

$$
51 \operatorname{div}  6 = 8 \, \textrm{R}\, {\color{red}{3}}
$$

So, our division gives $8$ wholes, and we're left with

$$
\dfrac{\color{red}3}{\color{blue}6}
$$

We can reduce the fraction

$$
\dfrac{\color{red}3}{\color{blue}6}
$$

to its lowest terms by dividing the numerator and denominator by $3{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{3}{6} &= \frac{3 \operatorname{div}  3}{6 \operatorname{div}  3} = \frac{1}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our mixed number is equivalent to

$$
8 \,\dfrac{1}{2}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186138118 :question/id #uuid "a5996998-a210-5da2-8b86-b3bf579d134a" :question/math-academy-id "e-13622" :question/problem "Which fraction is equivalent to $0.05$?" :question/worked-solution "Notice that $0.05$ has $2$ decimal places. So, we can write it as a fraction with $100$ in the denominator:

$$
0.05 = \dfrac{5}{100}
$$

We then reduce this fraction to its simplest form:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{5}{100} &= \frac{5 \operatorname{div}  5}{100 \operatorname{div}  5} \\
&= \frac{1}{100 \operatorname{div}  5} \\
&= \frac{1}{10 \cdot 10 \operatorname{div}  5} \\
&= (1)/(10 \cdot (10 \operatorname{div}  5)) \\
&= \frac{1}{10 \cdot 2} \\
&= \frac{1}{20}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $0.05$ is equivalent to

$$
\dfrac{1}{20}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186138120 :question/id #uuid "7d309af0-bf42-570a-bc5a-9dc01ca974d5" :question/math-academy-id "e-13636" :question/problem "What is the value of $\dfrac 3 8 + \dfrac 1 8$?" :question/worked-solution "To add two fractions with like denominators, we add the numerators and keep the denominators the same. Therefore,

$$
\frac{3}{8} + \frac{1}{8} = \frac{3 + 1}{8} = \frac{4}{8}
$$

We can simplify this fraction by dividing the numerator and the denominator by $4{:}$

$$
\dfrac{4}{8} = \dfrac{4\operatorname{div}  4}{8\operatorname{div}  4} = \dfrac{1}{2}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\dfrac 3 8 + \dfrac 1 8 = \dfrac 1 2
$$"} {:db/id 17592186138121 :question/id #uuid "f2d34ef1-81be-5999-9df2-9165bef2c53c" :question/math-academy-id "e-13637" :question/problem "Find the value of $\dfrac 2 3 + \dfrac 2 3$." :question/worked-solution "To add two fractions with like denominators, we add the numerators and keep the denominators the same. Therefore,

$$
\frac{2}{3} + \frac{2}{3} = \frac{2 + 2}{3} = \frac{4}{3}
$$

We then convert

$$
\dfrac 4 3
$$

to a mixed number:

$$
4\operatorname{div}  3 = 1\,\textrm{R}1 = 1\,\dfrac 1 3
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\dfrac 2 3 + \dfrac 2 3 = 1\,\dfrac 1 3
$$"} {:db/id 17592186138122 :question/id #uuid "44ca0914-a69b-5081-bc5a-7d8dd2af01b3" :question/math-academy-id "e-13679" :question/problem "What is the value of $5\,\dfrac{1}{2} + 2\,\dfrac 1 6$?" :question/worked-solution "To add two mixed numbers, we add whole numbers to whole numbers and fractions to fractions.

**Step 1**: Adding the whole numbers, we get

$$
5+2 = {\color{red}{7}}
$$

**Step 2**: Now we add the fractions:

$$
\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac 1 6
$$

To add two fractions with unlike denominators, we must express each fraction as an equivalent fraction with a common denominator.

Here, we can make a common denominator of $6$.

To put

$$
\dfrac 1 2
$$

over a denominator of $6$, we multiply the numerator and denominator by $3$:

$$
\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1\times 3}{2\times 3} = \dfrac{3}{6}
$$

We can now add the fractions. We keep the denominator the same, and we add the numerators.

$$
\frac{3}{6} + \frac{1}{6} = \frac{4}{6}
$$

Notice that we can simplify the above fraction by dividing the numerator and denominator by $2$:

$$
\dfrac{4}{6} = \dfrac{4\operatorname{div}  2}{6\operatorname{div}  2} = \color{blue} \dfrac{2}{3}
$$

**Step 3**: Combining our results gives:

$$
{\color{red}{7}} + {\color{blue}{\dfrac 2 3}} = 7\,\dfrac 2 3
$$"} {:db/id 17592186138124 :question/id #uuid "0bf56bec-fdab-5094-8d26-0b57e7522eb8" :question/math-academy-id "e-13682" :question/problem "Find the value of $1\,\dfrac{1}{2} + 3\,\dfrac 3 4$." :question/worked-solution "To add two mixed numbers, we add whole numbers to whole numbers and fractions to fractions.

**Step 1**: Adding the whole numbers, we get

$$
1+3 = {\color{red}{4}}
$$

**Step 2**: Now we add the fractions:

$$
\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac 3 4
$$

To add two fractions with unlike denominators, we must express each fraction as an equivalent fraction with a common denominator.

In this question, we can make a common denominator of $4$.

To put

$$
\dfrac 1 2
$$

over a denominator of $4$, we multiply the numerator and denominator by $2$:

$$
\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1\times 2}{2\times 2} = \dfrac{2}{4}
$$

We can now add the fractions. We keep the denominator the same, and we add the numerators.

$$
\frac{2}{4} + \frac{3}{4} = \frac{5}{4}
$$

Notice that this is an improper fraction. We can convert the fraction

$$
\dfrac{5}{4}
$$

to a mixed number in the usual way:

$$
5\operatorname{div}  4 = 1\,\textrm{R}1 = {\color{blue}{1\,\dfrac 1{4}}}
$$

**Step 3**: We combine the results to get our answer.

$$
{\color{red}{4}} + {\color{blue}{1\,\dfrac 1{4}}} = 5\,\dfrac 1{4}
$$

Notice that we needed to add the whole numbers one final time."} {:db/id 17592186138125 :question/id #uuid "f39c2dd0-f416-5bc4-b282-a732408716da" :question/math-academy-id "e-13686" :question/problem "Find the value of $\dfrac{2}{3} - \dfrac 1 6$." :question/worked-solution "To subtract two fractions with unlike denominators, we must express each fraction as an equivalent fraction with a common denominator.

Since $\color{blue}6$ is a multiple of ${\color{red}{3}}$, we can make a common denominator of ${\color{blue}{6}}$.

To put

$$
\dfrac 2 {\color{red}{3}}
$$

over a denominator of ${\color{blue}{6}}$, we multiply the numerator and denominator by $2$:

$$
\dfrac{2}{\color{red}3} = \dfrac{2\times 2}{{\color{red}{3}}\times 2} = \dfrac{4}{\color{blue}6}
$$

We can now subtract the fractions. We keep the denominator the same, and we subtract the numerators.

$$
\frac{4}{6} - \frac{1}{6} = \frac{3}{6}
$$

We can simplify this fraction by dividing the numerator and denominator by $3$:

$$
\dfrac{3\operatorname{div}  3}{6\operatorname{div}  3} = \dfrac{1}{2}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186138139 :question/id #uuid "8f412bc3-e3fb-56da-8ded-e201ca5086c5" :question/math-academy-id "e-13767" :question/problem "Evaluate $6\,\dfrac{1}{2} - 3\,\dfrac 3 {10}$." :question/worked-solution "To subtract two mixed numbers, we subtract whole numbers from whole numbers and fractions from fractions.

**Step 1**: Subtracting the whole numbers, we get

$$
6-3 = {\color{red}{3}}
$$

**Step 2**: Now we subtract the fractions:

$$
\dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac 3 {10}
$$

To subtract two fractions with unlike denominators, we need to express each fraction as an equivalent fraction with a common denominator.

In this example, we can make a common denominator of $10$.

To put

$$
\dfrac 1 2
$$

over a denominator of $10$, we multiply the numerator and denominator by $5$:

$$
\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1\times 5}{2\times 5} = \dfrac{5}{10}
$$

We can now subtract the fractions. We keep the denominator the same, and we subtract the numerators.

$$
\frac{5}{10} - \frac{3}{10} = \frac{2}{10}
$$

Next, we reduce the fraction to its lowest terms.

$$
\dfrac{2}{10} = \dfrac{2\operatorname{div}  2}{10\operatorname{div}  2} = \color{blue} \dfrac{1}{5}
$$

**Step 3**: We combine the results to get our final answer:

$$
{\color{red}3} + {\color{blue}{\dfrac 1 5}} = {\color{red}{3}}\,{\color{blue}{\dfrac 1 5}}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186138155 :question/id #uuid "135fa171-6d8d-508b-96b9-edca29e2aa54" :question/math-academy-id "e-13889" :question/problem "Calculate $256 \operatorname{div}  10$." :question/worked-solution "First, we write down our number. We can attach as many leading zeros to the whole number part as we want:

Therefore:

$$

$$

$$
\dfrac{7.47 \times 10}{1.2 \times 10} = \dfrac{74.7}{12}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{r@{\,}r} &  \\ 12 & \enclose{longdiv}{74{\bbox[2pt,lightgray]{\color{blue}{.}}}7}\end{array}

$$

$$

So,

$$
7.47 \operatorname{div}  1.2 = 6.225
$$

:question/problem "What is $0.7 \operatorname{div}  10$?"} {:db/id 17592186139623 :tutorial/content "We can use place value charts to divide decimals by $10$. For instance, to find the value of

$$
28 \operatorname{div}  10
$$

we perform the following steps.

**Step 1.** Write down the place value chart for $28$:



<div class="source-table-scroll"><table class="source-table" data-rules="all" data-table-align="center" data-frame="true">
<tbody><tr data-next-row="true">
<td data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8"><strong>tens</strong></td>
<td data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8"><strong>ones</strong></td>
<td data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8"></td>
<td data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8"><strong>tenths</strong></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td data-cell-align="center">$2$</td>
<td data-cell-align="center">$8$</td>
<td data-cell-align="center"><strong>.</strong></td>
<td data-cell-align="center"></td>
</tr>
</tbody></table></div>


**Step 2.** Move all digits by one place to the *right.*



<div class="source-table-scroll"><table class="source-table" data-rules="all" data-table-align="center" data-frame="true">
<tbody><tr data-next-row="true">
<td data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8"><strong>tens</strong></td>
<td data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8"><strong>ones</strong></td>
<td data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8"></td>
<td data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8"><strong>tenths</strong></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td data-cell-align="center"></td>
<td data-cell-align="center">$2$</td>
<td data-cell-align="center"><strong>.</strong></td>
<td data-cell-align="center">$8$</td>
</tr>
</tbody></table></div>


Therefore,

$$
28\operatorname{div}  10 = 2.8 \,
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6efc441f-c349-5538-bbf8-fc748aa7ddbd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1951 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186139624 :tutorial/content "When dividing by a power of ten, we shift the digits in the place value chart to the *right* by the number of zeros in the power of ten.

To illustrate, let's find the value of $47.2 \operatorname{div}  100$.

**Step 1.** Write down the place value chart for $47.2$:



<div class="source-table-scroll"><table class="source-table" data-rules="all" data-table-align="center" data-frame="true">
<tbody><tr data-next-row="true">
<td data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8"><strong>tens</strong></td>
<td data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8"><strong>ones</strong></td>
<td data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8"></td>
<td data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8"><strong>tenths</strong></td>
<td data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8"><strong>hundredths</strong></td>
<td data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8"><strong>thousandths</strong></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td data-cell-align="center">$4$</td>
<td data-cell-align="center">$7$</td>
<td data-cell-align="center"><strong>.</strong></td>
<td data-cell-align="center">$2$</td>
<td data-cell-align="center"></td>
<td data-cell-align="center"></td>
</tr>
</tbody></table></div>


**Step 2.** Determine the number of places to move. We're dividing by $100$, which has $\color{blue}2$ zeros, so we move all values to the *right* by $\color{blue}2$ places:



<div class="source-table-scroll"><table class="source-table" data-rules="all" data-table-align="center" data-frame="true">
<tbody><tr data-next-row="true">
<td data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8"><strong>tens</strong></td>
<td data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8"><strong>ones</strong></td>
<td data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8"></td>
<td data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8"><strong>tenths</strong></td>
<td data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8"><strong>hundredths</strong></td>
<td data-cell-align="center" data-fill="#D6EAF8"><strong>thousandths</strong></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td data-cell-align="center"></td>
<td data-cell-align="center"></td>
<td data-cell-align="center"><strong>.</strong></td>
<td data-cell-align="center">$4$</td>
<td data-cell-align="center">$7$</td>
<td data-cell-align="center">$2$</td>
</tr>
</tbody></table></div>


**Step 3.** Put zero in all empty cells that are to the right of the decimal point. We can also put a zero in the ones place if it is empty.
